metadata.title: Urinary incontinence in neurological disease: assessment and management
metadata.summary: This guideline addresses assessment and management of urinary incontinence and lower urinary tract dysfunction in children, young people and adults with neurological disease. It covers bladder storage and emptying, treatment selection, prevention of urinary tract infection, surveillance for complications and coordination of care, including the transition to adult services.

care_settings: Specialised care, including spinal injury units and paediatric urology units
target_population: Children, young people and adults with neurological disease and urinary incontinence or lower urinary tract dysfunction
therapeutic_areas: Bladder wall injection with botulinum toxin type A
Antibiotic prophylaxis for urinary tract infections
Bladder management with catheters, appliances or pads
Monitoring and surveillance of urinary tract complications

toxicities.event: Central nervous system effects, including confusion and possible cognitive impairment
prevention: When prescribing antimuscarinics, account for the potential central nervous system effects of agents that cross the blood-brain barrier, such as oxybutynin.

toxicities.event: Reduced bladder emptying and increased risk of urinary tract infection
prevention: After antimuscarinic treatment begins, check residual urine volume in people who do not use intermittent or indwelling catheterisation.
Consider the possibility of impaired bladder emptying and an increased urinary tract infection risk when prescribing antimuscarinics.
Account for the possibility that antimuscarinic treatment may cause or worsen constipation.

toxicities.event: Urinary retention after bladder wall injection
prevention: Before injection, explain that most people with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction need a catheterisation regimen after treatment, and confirm that the person and/or their family members and carers can and will manage one if retention occurs.
During treatment, monitor residual urine volume in people who do not use a catheterisation regimen.

toxicities.event: Long-term metabolic complications, including vitamin B12 deficiency
prevention: Provide lifelong follow-up after augmentation cystoplasty because long-term complications may occur.

recognition: Increased frequency of urinary tract infections
Other unexplained lower urinary tract symptoms

management.severity: Visible haematuria, increased frequency of urinary tract infections or other unexplained lower urinary tract symptoms
management.actions: Refer for urinary tract imaging and cystoscopy through a suspected cancer pathway referral.

prevention: Provide lifelong follow-up after augmentation cystoplasty because bladder cancer is a possible long-term complication.

Explain that people with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction may have an increased bladder cancer risk, particularly with a long history of dysfunction and complicating factors such as recurrent urinary tract infections; advise them to seek clinical assessment for warning symptoms, especially haematuria.
Do not routinely use synthetic tapes and slings for neurogenic stress incontinence because they carry a risk of urethral erosion.

toxicities.incidence: Can occur in some people after treatment of neurogenic stress incontinence.
prevention: Before insertion, ensure that the bladder can store urine adequately at low pressure.
Monitor the upper urinary tract after surgery, for example with annual ultrasound scans.

toxicities.event: Renal complications, including kidney stones, hydronephrosis, scarring and loss of kidney function
toxicities.incidence: Indwelling urethral catheters may carry a higher risk of renal complications, including kidney stones and scarring, than other bladder management methods such as intermittent self-catheterisation.
recognition: Hydronephrosis or kidney stones on imaging

management.severity: Symptoms suggesting upper urinary tract disease
Hydronephrosis or kidney stones on imaging, or biochemical evidence of renal deterioration

prevention: Explain the increased risk of renal complications to people with neurogenic urinary tract dysfunction, particularly those with spina bifida or spinal cord injury, and advise when to seek assessment for warning symptoms.
When discussing bladder management, explain the possible higher renal risk with indwelling urethral catheters.
Offer lifelong kidney ultrasound surveillance to people at high risk of renal complications; consider scans at annual or 2 yearly intervals.
During botulinum toxin type A treatment, monitor the upper urinary tract in people considered at risk of renal complications, such as those with high intravesical pressures on filling cystometry.

toxicities.incidence: Indwelling catheters (urethral and suprapubic) are associated with a higher incidence of bladder stones than other bladder management methods.
prevention: Discuss the increased bladder stone risk in neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction and the higher incidence associated with indwelling catheters; explain which symptoms warrant clinical assessment.
When changing a long-term indwelling urinary catheter, consider antibiotic prophylaxis for patients who experience trauma during catheterisation.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not use antibiotics routinely to prevent urinary tract infections. Consider prophylaxis for people with a recent history of frequent or severe urinary tract infections. Before prescribing, investigate treatable urinary tract causes, discuss benefits and risks with the person, and use microbiologist-approved local protocols or consult a microbiologist about the regimen. Regularly reassess whether prophylaxis remains necessary.
prophylaxis.target_population: People with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction; consideration of prophylaxis is limited to those with a recent history of frequent or severe urinary tract infections.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not provide antibiotics routinely when changing a long-term indwelling urinary catheter. Consider them if the patient has previously had a symptomatic urinary tract infection after a catheter change or experiences catheterisation trauma, defined by frank haematuria afterwards or 2 or more catheterisation attempts.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients undergoing a change of a long-term indwelling urinary catheter who have a history of symptomatic urinary tract infection after catheter change or experience trauma during catheterisation.

prophylaxis.recommendation: When considering ileal conduit diversion, discuss simultaneous cystectomy with the person as an option to prevent pyocystis.
prophylaxis.target_population: People with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction and intractable, major urinary tract management problems who are considering ileal conduit diversion.

infection_management.prevention: Do not routinely use antibiotic prophylaxis in neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction; consider it for a recent history of frequent or severe infections. Do not routinely give prophylactic antibiotics at long-term indwelling catheter changes, but consider them after a previous symptomatic infection following catheter change or when catheterisation causes trauma. Investigate treatable causes before starting prophylaxis and review any continuing prophylaxis regularly.
infection_management.management: If symptoms and urine dipstick findings suggest infection, obtain a urine bacterial culture and antibiotic sensitivity test before starting antibiotics. Treatment need not wait for results, but may be changed once they are available. Refer urgently for investigation of recurrent urinary tract infections, for example 3 or more infections in the last 6 months. In catheter users, bacterial colonisation can make dipstick tests and cultures unreliable for identifying active infection.

infection_management.prevention: Discuss simultaneous cystectomy as a preventive option when considering ileal conduit diversion.

therapies_index.name: behavioural management programme
approved_indications: May be considered for neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction after assessment by a healthcare professional trained in this condition, alongside education for the person and/or their family members and carers.
therapies_index.administration: The programme may use timed voiding, bladder retraining or habit retraining.

therapies_index.name: timed voiding
therapies_index.mechanism: Schedules urination at fixed intervals rather than in response to perceived bladder filling.
approved_indications: An option within a behavioural management programme for neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction.
therapies_index.administration: Urination is scheduled at set time intervals.

therapies_index.name: bladder retraining
therapies_index.mechanism: Gradually extends the time between voids or encourages a specified delay after the urge to void.
approved_indications: An option within a behavioural management programme for neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction.

therapies_index.name: habit retraining
therapies_index.mechanism: Uses an individual's toileting pattern to schedule voiding before expected incontinence episodes.
approved_indications: An option within a behavioural management programme for neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction; particularly suitable for people with cognitive impairment.

therapies_index.name: prompted voiding
therapies_index.mechanism: Encourages the person to initiate toileting, generally through education and positive reinforcement.
approved_indications: A behavioural management option particularly suitable for people with cognitive impairment.

therapies_index.name: antimuscarinic drugs
therapies_index.mechanism: Block muscarinic cholinergic receptors, reducing the bladder wall muscle's response to stimulating nerve impulses.
approved_indications: Offer for overactive bladder symptoms in people with spinal cord disease.
Consider for overactive bladder symptoms in people with conditions affecting the brain.
Consider when urodynamic investigations show impaired bladder storage.
key_toxicities: Reduced bladder emptying, which may increase the risk of urinary tract infections.
Effects outside the bladder may cause dry mouth.
Central nervous system effects may adversely affect cognitive function.
monitoring: Monitor residual urine volume after treatment begins in people not using intermittent or indwelling catheterisation.

therapies_index.name: oxybutynin
key_toxicities: As an example of an antimuscarinic that crosses the blood-brain barrier, it has the potential to cause central nervous system effects such as confusion.

therapies_index.name: beta-3-adrenoceptor agonists
approved_indications: The guideline points to NICE technology appraisal guidance on options for overactive bladder symptoms when antimuscarinics are unsuitable, insufficiently effective or cause unacceptable side effects.

therapies_index.name: vibegron
approved_indications: Referenced through NICE technology appraisal guidance as an option for overactive bladder symptoms when antimuscarinics are unsuitable, insufficiently effective or cause unacceptable side effects.

therapies_index.name: mirabegron
approved_indications: Referenced through NICE technology appraisal guidance as an option for overactive bladder symptoms when antimuscarinics are unsuitable, insufficiently effective or cause unacceptable side effects.

therapies_index.name: botulinum toxin type A
approved_indications: Offer bladder wall injection to adults with spinal cord disease and overactive bladder symptoms when antimuscarinic drugs have been ineffective or poorly tolerated.
Consider bladder wall injection for children and young people with spinal cord disease and overactive bladder symptoms when antimuscarinic drugs have been ineffective or poorly tolerated.
Offer bladder wall injection to adults with spinal cord disease and urodynamically demonstrated impaired bladder storage when antimuscarinic drugs have been ineffective or poorly tolerated.

Consider bladder wall injection for children and young people with spinal cord disease and urodynamically demonstrated impaired bladder storage when antimuscarinic drugs have been ineffective or poorly tolerated.
therapies_index.administration: Injected into the bladder wall; repeated injections may be provided when symptoms return.
monitoring: Monitor residual urine volume during treatment in people who are not using a catheterisation regimen.
Monitor the upper urinary tract during treatment in people considered at risk of renal complications.

therapies_index.name: augmentation cystoplasty
therapies_index.mechanism: Uses an isolated intestinal segment to increase bladder capacity.
approved_indications: Consider for complications of impaired bladder storage in people with non-progressive neurological disorders, only after thorough clinical and urodynamic assessment and discussion of complications, risks and alternatives.
therapies_index.administration: Surgical bladder reconstruction using an intestinal segment.
key_toxicities: Long-term metabolic effects, including vitamin B12 deficiency.
monitoring: Provide lifelong follow-up because of the risk of long-term complications.

therapies_index.name: pelvic floor muscle training
therapies_index.mechanism: Strengthens muscles that support the pelvic organs and help prevent involuntary urine leakage.
approved_indications: Consider for lower urinary tract dysfunction due to multiple sclerosis or stroke, or another neurological condition in which voluntary pelvic floor contraction is preserved.
therapies_index.administration: A daily training programme; select patients after specialist pelvic floor assessment and consider combining it with biofeedback and/or electrical stimulation of the pelvic floor.

therapies_index.name: biofeedback
therapies_index.mechanism: Uses instrument-based information about physiological activity to help the person recognise and voluntarily influence that activity.
approved_indications: May be combined with pelvic floor muscle training in selected people.

therapies_index.name: electrical stimulation of the pelvic floor
approved_indications: May be combined with pelvic floor muscle training in selected people.

therapies_index.name: neuromuscular electrical stimulation
therapies_index.mechanism: Electrical impulses delivered through the skin stimulate underlying nerves and muscles to produce involuntary contractions.
therapies_index.administration: Small electrical impulses are delivered through the skin.

therapies_index.name: autologous fascial sling surgery
therapies_index.mechanism: Supports the urethra with a harvested strip of rectus fascia.
approved_indications: Consider for neurogenic stress incontinence.
therapies_index.administration: A surgically placed strip of the person's rectus fascia supports the urethra.

therapies_index.name: artificial urinary sphincter
approved_indications: Consider insertion for neurogenic stress incontinence only when an alternative procedure, such as an autologous fascial sling, is less likely to control incontinence.
therapies_index.administration: Surgical insertion requires an assessment that the bladder has adequate low-pressure storage capacity and a discussion of device risks, possible repeat operations and alternatives.
key_toxicities: Bladder storage function can deteriorate after treatment.
monitoring: Monitor the upper urinary tract after surgery, for example with annual ultrasound scans.

therapies_index.name: alpha-blockers
therapies_index.mechanism: Block alpha receptor responses to sympathetic impulses, inhibiting contraction of non-vascular smooth muscle, including at the bladder neck and within the prostate.

therapies_index.name: catheter valve
approved_indications: May be used instead of a drainage bag when appropriate for the person.
therapies_index.administration: Suitability takes account of preference, support from family members and carers, manual dexterity, cognitive ability and lower urinary tract function.
monitoring: Consider continued upper urinary tract surveillance in people with impaired bladder storage.

therapies_index.name: ileal conduit diversion
therapies_index.mechanism: Diverts urine from the ureters to an abdominal stoma through an isolated segment of small intestine.
approved_indications: Consider for neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction with major, intractable urinary tract management problems, such as incontinence or renal deterioration.
therapies_index.administration: Surgical urinary diversion; discuss the option of simultaneous cystectomy as prophylaxis against pyocystis.

therapies_index.name: cystectomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Removes all or part of the urinary bladder.
approved_indications: Discuss simultaneous cystectomy as an option to prevent pyocystis when considering ileal conduit diversion.
therapies_index.administration: Surgical removal of all or part of the bladder.

therapies_index.name: antibiotic prophylaxis
approved_indications: Do not use routinely to prevent urinary tract infections in people with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction.
Consider for people with a recent history of frequent or severe urinary tract infections.

Do not offer routinely when changing a long-term indwelling urinary catheter; consider for people with a history of symptomatic urinary tract infection after catheter change or trauma during catheterisation.
therapies_index.administration: Before prescribing, investigate treatable urinary tract causes, discuss risks and benefits, and consult microbiologist-approved local protocols or a microbiologist about suitable regimens.
monitoring: Regularly review whether ongoing prophylaxis is needed.

therapies_index.name: antibiotic treatment
approved_indications: Treatment may begin when symptoms and urine dipstick findings suggest infection, after arranging urine bacterial culture and antibiotic sensitivity testing.
therapies_index.administration: Treatment need not await culture results but may be adjusted when they become available.

therapies_index.name: intermittent self-catheterisation
approved_indications: Mentioned as a bladder management strategy rather than given a specific recommendation for initiation.
therapies_index.administration: People starting or using a catheter-based bladder management system should receive training, support and review from appropriately trained healthcare professionals.
monitoring: Review products at intervals no longer than 2 years.

therapies_index.name: indwelling urethral catheters
approved_indications: Mentioned as a bladder management strategy rather than given a specific recommendation for initiation.
key_toxicities: May be associated with higher risks of renal complications, including kidney stones and scarring, than other bladder management methods.
Indwelling urethral and suprapubic catheters are associated with a higher incidence of bladder stones than other bladder management methods.
monitoring: Review catheter-related products at intervals no longer than 2 years.

therapies_index.name: suprapubic catheterisation
approved_indications: Mentioned as a bladder management strategy rather than given a specific recommendation for initiation.
key_toxicities: Indwelling urethral and suprapubic catheters are associated with a higher incidence of bladder stones than other bladder management methods.
monitoring: Review catheter-related products at intervals no longer than 2 years.

therapies_index.name: penile sheath collection systems
approved_indications: Mentioned as a bladder management strategy; no specific recommendation for its use is given.

therapies_index.name: pads
approved_indications: Mentioned as a bladder management product; no specific recommendation for its initiation is given.
therapies_index.administration: People using pads should have access to products suited to their needs and receive support from healthcare professionals trained in the relevant bladder management systems.
monitoring: Review products at intervals no longer than 2 years.

conditions.name: neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction
conditions.description: Neurological disease can disrupt coordinated urine storage or bladder emptying. The pattern of bladder and sphincter dysfunction varies with the location and nature of nervous system damage.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Symptoms can involve impaired storage, difficulty emptying the bladder, or both. Increased urinary frequency and incontinence can affect daily activities and social participation. Bowel and sexual dysfunction may coexist. Urinary tract infection, high bladder pressures and kidney stones can contribute to loss of kidney function.

subtypes.name: impaired bladder storage
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May cause increased urinary frequency or incontinence; adverse urodynamic features include impaired bladder compliance.

subtypes.name: neurogenic stress incontinence
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Incontinence associated with increased abdominal pressure rather than a detrusor contraction; a diagnosis of urodynamic stress incontinence requires urodynamic investigation.

subtypes.name: bladder emptying problems caused by neurological disease
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Difficulty emptying the bladder may leave residual urine.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish urinary and neurological symptoms, the neurological diagnosis and its course, bowel symptoms, sexual function, comorbidities, and medication and therapy use.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At assessment of lower urinary tract dysfunction, including new presentations, changing symptoms and periodic reassessment.

diagnostic_workup.test: Assessment of mobility, hand function, cognitive function, social support and lifestyle
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify factors affecting the feasibility of bladder management.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During clinical assessment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure blood pressure and examine the abdomen and external genitalia; perform vaginal or rectal examination when clinically indicated to assess findings such as pelvic floor prolapse, faecal loading or altered anal tone.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During clinical assessment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess relevant cognitive function, walking and mobility, hand function, and lumbar and sacral spinal segment function.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During clinical assessment, with components selected as needed.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Check for blood, glucose, protein, leukocytes and nitrites.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use an appropriately obtained sample; acceptable sources include clean-catch midstream urine, a freshly inserted intermittent sterile catheter or a catheter port, but not a leg bag.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Catheter-associated bacterial colonisation can make dipstick results unreliable for identifying active infection.

diagnostic_workup.test: Urine bacterial culture and antibiotic sensitivity test
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate suspected urinary tract infection and inform antibiotic treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Arrange before antibiotics when symptoms and dipstick findings suggest infection; treatment need not wait for the result.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Catheter-associated bacterial colonisation can make culture unreliable for diagnosing active infection.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Record fluid intake, urinary frequency and voided volume.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Ask the person and their family members or carers to record information for a minimum of 3 days.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess urinary flow.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider for people able to void voluntarily.

diagnostic_workup.test: Post-void residual urine volume by ultrasound
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure urine remaining after voiding and assess variation in bladder emptying.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Measure during assessment, preferably with a portable scanner; consider repeat measurements on different occasions.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the kidneys for complications.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider referral for people at high risk of renal complications, including those with spina bifida or spinal cord injury.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate lower urinary tract function during filling and emptying.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Offer to people known to have a high risk of renal complications, such as those with spina bifida, spinal cord injury or anorectal abnormalities.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess lower urinary tract function, including bladder storage.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Offer before surgery for neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction; consider during surveillance for people at high risk of urinary tract complications. Do not offer routinely to those known to have a low risk of renal complications, such as most people with multiple sclerosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Impaired bladder compliance, detrusorsphincter dyssynergia or vesico-ureteric reflux identify adverse features relevant to renal risk.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate possible upper urinary tract disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use when symptoms suggest upper urinary tract disease.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Obtain an accurate measurement of glomerular filtration rate.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider when an accurate measurement is needed, for example if kidney imaging suggests compromised renal function.

follow_up.schedule: The interval for routine reassessment depends on individual circumstances but should not exceed 3 years. Offer lifelong kidney ultrasound surveillance to people judged at high risk of renal complications, with annual or 2 yearly intervals given as examples.
recommended_tests: Kidney ultrasound for people at high risk of renal complications
Consider urodynamic investigations during surveillance for people at high risk of urinary tract complications
Do not use plain abdominal radiography, cystoscopy or renal scintigraphy for routine surveillance
Do not use serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate alone to monitor renal function
long_term_effects: Kidney stones, hydronephrosis and renal scarring
Possible increased risk of bladder cancer, particularly with longstanding dysfunction and complicating factors
follow_up.survivorship_notes: High-risk groups include people with spinal cord injury or spina bifida and those with impaired bladder compliance, detrusorsphincter dyssynergia or vesico-ureteric reflux on urodynamic testing.

conditions.name: overactive bladder
conditions.description: A bladder symptom pattern characterised by urgency, with or without urge incontinence, usually accompanied by increased urinary frequency.
conditions.clinical_presentation: A sudden, strong need to urinate may occur with frequency and incontinence.

diagnostic_workup.test: Clinical assessment of urinary symptoms and neurological disease
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify overactive bladder symptoms and whether the neurological condition affects the spinal cord or brain.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When assessing symptoms such as frequency, urgency or incontinence.

diagnostic_workup.test: Post-void residual urine volume by ultrasound
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Monitor bladder emptying.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Monitor after starting antimuscarinic treatment in people not using intermittent or indwelling catheterisation, and during botulinum toxin type A treatment in people not using a catheterisation regimen.

recommended_tests: Residual urine volume monitoring when indicated during antimuscarinic or botulinum toxin type A treatment
Upper urinary tract monitoring during botulinum toxin type A treatment for people judged at risk of renal complications
follow_up.survivorship_notes: People receiving repeated botulinum toxin type A injections should have prompt access to another injection when symptoms recur.

conditions.name: impaired bladder storage
conditions.description: A disturbance of the bladder's urine-storage function that may be demonstrated by urodynamic investigation.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Storage dysfunction can cause increased urinary frequency or incontinence; complications may include hydronephrosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify impaired storage and adverse findings such as impaired bladder compliance or high intravesical pressures.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Used to establish storage dysfunction and as part of the assessment before surgical treatment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Impaired bladder compliance and high intravesical pressures are relevant to the risk of upper urinary tract complications.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess complications affecting the kidneys and upper urinary tract.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider surveillance when bladder storage is impaired and monitor during botulinum toxin type A treatment if renal complications are a concern.

recommended_tests: Consider continuing upper urinary tract surveillance when storage is impaired, including when a catheter valve is used
Monitor the upper urinary tract during botulinum toxin type A treatment when renal complication risk is identified
long_term_effects: Renal complications associated with high intravesical pressures

conditions.name: neurogenic stress incontinence
conditions.description: Stress urinary incontinence occurring in the setting of neurological disease.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Involuntary urine leakage occurs with increased abdominal pressure; urodynamic stress incontinence is distinguished by the absence of a detrusor contraction.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish a diagnosis of urodynamic stress incontinence and assess function before surgery.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Required to diagnose urodynamic stress incontinence; offer before surgery for neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Urine leakage during increased abdominal pressure without a detrusor contraction meets the document's definition of urodynamic stress incontinence.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Select people for pelvic floor muscle training.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before selecting this training.

diagnostic_workup.test: Assessment of low-pressure bladder storage capacity
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine whether bladder storage is adequate.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When considering insertion of an artificial urinary sphincter.

follow_up.schedule: After artificial urinary sphincter surgery, monitor the upper urinary tract; annual ultrasound scans are given as an example.
recommended_tests: Upper urinary tract ultrasound after artificial urinary sphincter surgery
long_term_effects: Bladder storage function can deteriorate after treatment

conditions.name: bladder emptying problems caused by neurological disease
conditions.description: Difficulty emptying the bladder attributable to neurological disease.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Incomplete emptying may occur and is a predisposing factor for urinary tract infection.

diagnostic_workup.test: Post-void residual urine volume by ultrasound
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Quantify urine remaining after voiding and identify variation in emptying.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Measure during assessment and consider measurements on different occasions.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess flow during voluntary voiding.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider when the person can void voluntarily.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess bladder emptying using simultaneous measurements of bladder pressure and urinary flow.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Low urinary flow together with raised bladder pressure during voiding can indicate bladder outflow obstruction.

long_term_effects: Urinary tract infections associated with incomplete bladder emptying

conditions.name: urinary tract infections
conditions.description: Urinary infections are a recognised complication of neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction.
conditions.epidemiology: The document describes a markedly increased infection risk in people with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction but gives no numerical rate.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Infection may worsen incontinence or cause malaise, and may extend to the upper urinary tract with possible loss of renal function. Fever associated with infection may worsen neurological function in some neurological diseases. Recurrent infection can be a warning sign of urinary tract complications.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Check for blood, glucose, protein, leukocytes and nitrites.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use an appropriately collected sample when assessing urinary tract dysfunction.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: In catheter users, bacterial colonisation can limit its reliability for diagnosing active infection.

diagnostic_workup.test: Urine bacterial culture and antibiotic sensitivity test
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate suspected infection and guide antibiotic treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Arrange before antibiotic treatment when symptoms and dipstick findings suggest infection; treatment does not have to be delayed.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Catheter-associated bacterial colonisation can limit the reliability of culture for identifying active infection.

diagnostic_workup.test: Urinary tract investigation for a treatable underlying cause
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Look for contributors such as urinary tract stones or incomplete bladder emptying.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before prescribing antibiotic prophylaxis.

follow_up.schedule: Regularly review whether ongoing antibiotic prophylaxis remains needed in everyone receiving it.
long_term_effects: Possible upper urinary tract involvement and loss of renal function
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Recurrent urinary tract infections, for example 3 or more infections in the last 6 months, warrant urgent investigation.

conditions.name: renal impairment
conditions.description: Kidney function may deteriorate as a complication of neurogenic urinary tract dysfunction.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Potential renal complications include kidney stones, hydronephrosis and scarring. Loin pain, urinary tract infection, haematuria, imaging abnormalities or biochemical evidence of deterioration may signal a problem.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate symptoms suggesting upper urinary tract disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Use when upper urinary tract disease is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Hydronephrosis or kidney stones on imaging are signs warranting urgent investigation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess and surveil renal complications.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider during initial assessment for people at high renal risk; offer lifelong surveillance to those judged at high risk.

diagnostic_workup.test: Serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Monitor renal function.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When monitoring people with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Do not rely on these measurements in isolation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure glomerular filtration rate accurately.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider when an accurate value is needed, such as when renal imaging suggests impaired function.

follow_up.schedule: Offer lifelong kidney ultrasound surveillance to people judged at high risk; annual or 2 yearly scanning is given as an example.
recommended_tests: Kidney ultrasound in people at high risk of renal complications
follow_up.survivorship_notes: People with spina bifida or spinal cord injury are highlighted as being at increased renal risk. The document cautions that indwelling urethral catheters may carry higher risks of kidney stones and scarring than other bladder-management methods.

conditions.name: bladder stones
conditions.description: Urinary bladder stones form through crystallisation of substances in urine; the document notes that formation commonly accompanies bacterial colonisation or incomplete bladder emptying.
conditions.epidemiology: People with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction have increased risk. Indwelling urethral and suprapubic catheters are associated with a higher incidence than other forms of bladder management.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Recurrent infection, repeated catheter blockage or haematuria may suggest a bladder stone.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate suspected bladder stones.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Refer when symptoms suggest stones, including recurrent catheter blockage, recurrent urinary tract infection or haematuria.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: People and their family members or carers should be informed about symptoms that warrant assessment.

conditions.name: bladder cancer
conditions.description: A potential complication of longstanding neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction.
conditions.epidemiology: The document states that risk may be increased, particularly in people with a long history of neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction and complicating factors such as recurrent urinary tract infections; it provides no incidence estimate.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Haematuria, especially visible haematuria, increased urinary tract infection frequency or other unexplained lower urinary tract symptoms may prompt investigation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate possible bladder cancer.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Refer through a suspected cancer pathway when there is visible haematuria, increased frequency of urinary tract infections or other unexplained lower urinary tract symptoms.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: Inform people and their family members or carers about symptoms, particularly haematuria, that warrant medical assessment. Cystoscopy is not recommended for routine surveillance of neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction.

artifacts.summary: The table groups neurological conditions by lesion location and whether they are congenital or perinatal, acquired and stable, or acquired and progressive or degenerative.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Lesion location and disease course help clinicians anticipate patterns of bladder and sphincter dysfunction when assessing urinary symptoms.

special_populations.considerations: Plan a structured transfer early, involving the young person and their parents or carers. Receiving services should review the documentation, coordinate with other adult services, provide contact details and ensure that urological care continues. Consider regular meetings between paediatric and adult specialists before and after transfer.

special_populations.population: People at high risk of renal complications
special_populations.considerations: Examples include people with spinal cord injury or spina bifida and those with adverse urodynamic features, such as impaired bladder compliance, detrusorsphincter dyssynergia or vesico-ureteric reflux. Other assessment examples include anorectal abnormalities. Renal risk also affects monitoring during botulinum toxin type A treatment.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Offer video-urodynamic investigations to those known to be at high risk; offer lifelong kidney ultrasound surveillance, for example at annual or 2 yearly intervals. special_populations.population: People with a long-term indwelling urinary catheter

special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not offer antibiotic prophylaxis routinely at catheter change; consider it when either specified risk factor is present.

recommendations.statement: Consider pelvic floor muscle training for lower urinary tract dysfunction due to multiple sclerosis or stroke, or another neurological condition when voluntary pelvic floor contraction is preserved. Select patients after specialist pelvic floor assessment and consider adding biofeedback and/or pelvic floor electrical stimulation.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.4 Treatment for stress incontinence — Pelvic floor muscle training

recommendations.statement: Consider autologous fascial sling surgery for neurogenic stress incontinence.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.4 Treatment for stress incontinence — Urethral tape and sling surgery

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely use synthetic tapes or slings for neurogenic stress incontinence because they carry a risk of urethral erosion.
recommendations.rationale: Synthetic tapes and slings carry a risk of urethral erosion.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.4 Treatment for stress incontinence — Urethral tape and sling surgery

recommendations.statement: Consider implantation of an artificial urinary sphincter for neurogenic stress incontinence only when another procedure, such as an autologous fascial sling, is less likely to control the incontinence.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.4 Treatment for stress incontinence — Artificial urinary sphincter

recommendations.statement: When considering an artificial urinary sphincter, discuss device-related risks, possible repeat surgery and alternative procedures with the person and/or their family and carers, and ensure the bladder can store an adequate volume at low pressure.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.4 Treatment for stress incontinence — Artificial urinary sphincter

recommendations.statement: After artificial urinary sphincter surgery, monitor the upper urinary tract, for example with annual ultrasound scans.
recommendations.rationale: Bladder storage function may worsen in some people after treatment of neurogenic stress incontinence.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.4 Treatment for stress incontinence — Artificial urinary sphincter

recommendations.statement: Do not offer alpha-blockers to treat bladder emptying problems caused by neurological disease.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.5 Treatment to improve bladder emptying — Alpha-blockers

recommendations.statement: A catheter valve may be used instead of a drainage bag when appropriate for the person.
recommendations.context: This recommendation originates from the NICE guideline on healthcare-associated infections: prevention and control in primary and community care.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.6 Management with catheter valves

recommendations.statement: Before offering a catheter valve in place of continuous drainage into a bag, consider the person's preference, support from family and carers, manual dexterity, cognition and lower urinary tract function.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.6 Management with catheter valves

recommendations.statement: Consider whether ongoing upper urinary tract surveillance is needed for people with impaired bladder storage, such as reduced bladder compliance.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.6 Management with catheter valves

recommendations.statement: For people with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction and severe, intractable urinary management problems, such as incontinence or renal deterioration, consider ileal conduit diversion (urostomy) and discuss simultaneous cystectomy as prophylaxis against pyocystis.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.7 Management with ileal conduit diversion

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely use antibiotic prophylaxis against urinary tract infections in people with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.8 Treatment to prevent urinary tract infection

recommendations.statement: Consider antibiotic prophylaxis for people with a recent history of frequent or severe urinary tract infections.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.8 Treatment to prevent urinary tract infection

recommendations.statement: Before prescribing antibiotic prophylaxis for urinary tract infection, investigate treatable underlying urinary tract causes, such as stones or incomplete emptying; discuss prophylaxis risks and benefits with the person; and consult microbiologist-approved local protocols or a microbiologist about suitable regimens.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.8 Treatment to prevent urinary tract infection

recommendations.statement: Regularly reassess whether antibiotic prophylaxis remains necessary for every person receiving it.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.8 Treatment to prevent urinary tract infection

recommendations.statement: When changing a long-term indwelling urinary catheter, do not routinely provide antibiotic prophylaxis. Consider it if the person has previously had a symptomatic urinary tract infection after catheter change or experiences catheterisation trauma, defined as frank haematuria afterwards or 2 or more catheterisation attempts.
recommendations.context: This recommendation originates from the NICE guideline on healthcare-associated infections: prevention and control in primary and community care. In August 2012, no antibiotics had UK marketing authorisation for this indication.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.8 Treatment to prevent urinary tract infection

recommendations.statement: Do not monitor renal function in neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction using serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate alone.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.9 Monitoring and surveillance protocols

recommendations.statement: Consider isotopic glomerular filtration rate when an accurate measurement is needed, for example when kidney imaging suggests renal function may be compromised.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.9 Monitoring and surveillance protocols

recommendations.statement: Offer lifelong kidney ultrasound surveillance to people judged at high risk of renal complications; for example, consider scans at annual or 2 yearly intervals. High-risk groups include people with spinal cord injury or spina bifida and those with adverse urodynamic findings such as impaired bladder compliance, detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia or vesico-ureteric reflux.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.9 Monitoring and surveillance protocols

recommendations.statement: Do not use plain abdominal radiography for routine surveillance of people with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.9 Monitoring and surveillance protocols

recommendations.statement: Consider including urodynamic investigations in surveillance for people at high risk of urinary tract complications, such as those with spina bifida, spinal cord injury or anorectal abnormalities.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.9 Monitoring and surveillance protocols

recommendations.statement: Do not use cystoscopy for routine surveillance in neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.9 Monitoring and surveillance protocols

recommendations.statement: Do not use renal scintigraphy for routine surveillance in neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.9 Monitoring and surveillance protocols

recommendations.statement: Discuss the increased risk of renal complications, including stones, hydronephrosis and scarring, with people who have neurogenic urinary tract dysfunction and their families and carers, particularly in spina bifida or spinal cord injury. Explain warning symptoms, including loin pain, urinary tract infection and haematuria, and when to seek professional care.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.10 Potential complications: providing information and initial management — Renal impairment

recommendations.statement: When discussing treatment choices, explain that indwelling urethral catheters may carry greater risks of renal complications, such as stones and scarring, than other bladder management approaches, such as intermittent self-catheterisation.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.10 Potential complications: providing information and initial management — Renal impairment

recommendations.statement: Investigate symptoms suggestive of upper urinary tract disease with renal imaging.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.10 Potential complications: providing information and initial management — Renal impairment

recommendations.statement: Discuss the increased risk of bladder stones in neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction with the person and their family and carers. Explain that recurrent infection, repeated catheter blockage or haematuria should prompt contact with a healthcare professional.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.10 Potential complications: providing information and initial management — Bladder stones

recommendations.statement: Explain to the person and their family and carers that urethral and suprapubic indwelling catheters are associated with a higher incidence of bladder stones than other bladder management approaches. Advise them to seek professional care for symptoms such as recurrent infection, recurrent catheter blockage or haematuria.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.10 Potential complications: providing information and initial management — Bladder stones

recommendations.statement: Refer for cystoscopy when symptoms suggest bladder stones, such as recurrent catheter blockage, recurrent urinary tract infection or haematuria.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.10 Potential complications: providing information and initial management — Bladder stones

recommendations.statement: Discuss with the person and their family and carers the possibility of increased bladder cancer risk in neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction, particularly after a long history of dysfunction with complicating factors such as recurrent urinary tract infections. Explain which symptoms, especially haematuria, warrant professional assessment.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.10 Potential complications: providing information and initial management — Bladder cancer

recommendations.statement: Use a suspected cancer pathway referral for urinary tract imaging and cystoscopy when a person has visible haematuria, an increased frequency of urinary tract infections or other unexplained lower urinary tract symptoms.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.10 Potential complications: providing information and initial management — Bladder cancer

recommendations.statement: If a person has received specialised care for neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction, give specialist-advice contact details to them, their family and carers, and the non-specialist medical and nursing staff caring for them.
recommendations.context: Specialised settings include a spinal injury unit or paediatric urology unit.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.11 Access to and interaction with services

recommendations.statement: Provide people with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction and their family and carers written information listing key care professionals, their roles and contact details, copies of clinical correspondence, and prescribed medicines and equipment. Send the information to the person's GP as well.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.11 Access to and interaction with services

recommendations.statement: Healthcare professionals should follow the NICE guideline on patient experience in adult NHS services, particularly its recommendations on tailoring services to individuals and maintaining continuity of care and relationships.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.11 Access to and interaction with services

recommendations.statement: When transferring a person with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction from paediatric to adult services, establish a clear, structured care pathway early with the person and their parents and carers. With the young person's consent, involve parents and carers in transfer documentation; give the person and receiving clinician a full account of clinical history, investigations and treatment; incorporate multidisciplinary team information; plan continuing urological services; and formally transfer responsibility to named individual(s).
recommendations.source_heading: 1.11 Access to and interaction with services — Transfer from child to adult services

recommendations.statement: When accepting a person with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction into adult services, review the transfer documents and coordinate with other adult services involved in ongoing care. Give the person the receiving service's details and contacts for key staff, including the urologist and specialist nurses, and ensure urological services continue after transition.
recommendations.source_heading: 1.11 Access to and interaction with services — Transfer from child to adult services

recommendations.statement: Consider regular multidisciplinary meetings between paediatric and adult specialists to discuss management of neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction in children and young people during the years before transfer and after entry into adult services.
