document_sections.heading: Your responsibility
document_sections.content: NICE recommendations should inform professional judgement alongside each person's needs, preferences and values. They are not mandatory and do not replace individualised decisions made with the person and, where appropriate, their family, carers or guardian. Problems involving a medicine or medical device used in treatment or a procedure should be reported to the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency through the Yellow Card Scheme.

document_sections.heading: Overview
document_sections.content: This guideline addresses assessment and management of urinary incontinence in children, young people and adults with neurological disease. It aims to improve care by relating treatment choices to symptoms and neurological conditions.

document_sections.heading: Who is it for?
document_sections.content: The intended readers are healthcare professionals, commissioners and providers, and people with urinary incontinence and neurological disease together with their families and carers.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: People should participate in discussions and informed decisions about their care. NICE explains elsewhere how its wording conveys the strength or certainty of recommendations and addresses prescribing, consent, mental capacity and safeguarding.

document_sections.heading: 1.1 Assessment of lower urinary tract dysfunction in patients with neurological conditions
document_sections.content: Assessment is relevant at first presentation, when symptoms change and when urinary tract management needs periodic review. Routine reassessment intervals depend on individual circumstances, including age, diagnosis and management method, but should not exceed 3 years. These assessment recommendations concern people with a neurological condition; when assessment identifies non-neurogenic incontinence, management guidance is available in the NICE guidelines for lower urinary tract symptoms in men and for urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women.

document_sections.heading: Clinical assessment
document_sections.content: 1.1.1 Obtain a history covering urinary symptoms, neurological symptoms and any known diagnosis, the course of neurological disease, bowel symptoms, sexual function, comorbidities, and prescribed or other medicines and therapies. 1.1.2 Determine how neurological disease affects mobility, hand function, cognition, social support and lifestyle, because these factors influence management. 1.1.3 Perform a general examination that includes blood pressure, abdomen and external genitalia; add vaginal or rectal examination when clinically indicated, for example to assess pelvic floor prolapse, faecal loading or anal tone. 1.1.4 Perform a focused neurological examination, potentially covering cognition, walking and mobility, hand function, and lumbar and sacral spinal segment function. 1.1.5 Test an appropriately obtained urine sample by dipstick for blood, glucose, protein, leukocytes and nitrites. Suitable sources are a clean-catch midstream sample, a newly inserted intermittent sterile catheter or a catheter port; do not sample a leg bag. 1.1.6 If symptoms and dipstick findings suggest infection, arrange bacterial culture and antibiotic sensitivity testing before antibiotics begin; treatment does not have to await results and can be adjusted afterwards. 1.1.7 Catheter users have bacterial colonisation, making dipstick results and culture potentially unreliable indicators of active infection. 1.1.8 Ask the person and their family or carers to chart fluid intake, voiding frequency and urine volume for a minimum of 3 days. 1.1.9 Consider flow-rate measurement when voluntary voiding is possible. 1.1.10 Measure post-void residual urine by ultrasound, preferably with a portable scanner, and consider repeat measurements on separate occasions to identify variation in emptying. 1.1.11 Consider referral for renal ultrasound when renal complication risk is high, as with spina bifida or spinal cord injury. 1.1.12 Arrange urgent investigation for haematuria; recurrent urinary tract infections, for example 3 or more infections in the last 6 months; loin pain; repeated catheter obstruction, for example blockage within 6 weeks of a change; hydronephrosis or kidney stones on imaging; or biochemical evidence of worsening renal function. 1.1.13 Unexplained neurological changes, such as confusion or increased spasticity, can reflect urinary tract disease; consider further urinary investigation and treatment when suspected. 1.1.14 Refer changes in urinary function that could reflect a new or progressive neurological disease requiring specialist investigation, such as syringomyelia, hydrocephalus, multiple system atrophy or cauda equina syndrome. 1.1.15 Assess effects of urinary symptoms on family and carers and consider reducing harm; follow local safeguarding procedures if severe stress is suspected of leading to abuse.

document_sections.heading: Urodynamic investigations
document_sections.content: 1.1.16 Do not routinely offer urodynamic testing, including filling cystometry or pressure-flow studies, to people known to have low renal complication risk, such as most people with multiple sclerosis. 1.1.17 Offer video-urodynamic assessment to those known to have high renal complication risk, including people with spina bifida, spinal cord injury or anorectal abnormalities. 1.1.18 Offer urodynamic assessment before surgery for neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction.

document_sections.heading: 1.2 Information and support
document_sections.content: 1.2.1 Offer condition-specific information and training to people with neurogenic urinary tract dysfunction and their families and carers. For users starting or continuing catheters, appliances or pads, ensure training, support and review by professionals familiar with the relevant management systems and available products; provide products meeting individual needs and review them at a maximum of 2 yearly intervals. 1.2.2 Adapt information and training to physical abilities and cognition to support participation and self-management. 1.2.3 Explain how to obtain further professional advice about urinary tract management. 1.2.4 Healthcare professionals should follow the NICE guideline on patient experience in adult NHS services; related NICE guidance addresses shared decision making and information that supports active involvement in care.

document_sections.heading: 1.3 Treatment to improve bladder storage
document_sections.content: This section addresses behavioural treatment, medicines, botulinum toxin type A and augmentation cystoplasty for impaired bladder storage.

document_sections.heading: Behavioural treatments
document_sections.content: 1.3.1 Consider a behavioural programme, such as timed voiding, bladder retraining or habit retraining, for neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction only after assessment by a professional trained in this condition and together with education about lower urinary tract function for the person or their family and carers. 1.3.2 When selecting a programme, recognise that prompted voiding and habit retraining are particularly appropriate for cognitive impairment.

document_sections.heading: Pharmacological treatments
document_sections.content: The pharmacological options discussed are antimuscarinics and beta-3-adrenoceptor agonists.

document_sections.heading: Antimuscarinics
document_sections.content: In August 2012, not every antimuscarinic had UK marketing authorisation for the uses in recommendations 1.3.3 to 1.3.5 or for both adults and children. 1.3.3 Offer antimuscarinic drugs when spinal cord disease, such as spinal cord injury or multiple sclerosis, occurs with overactive bladder symptoms including frequency, urgency and incontinence. 1.3.4 Consider them when a condition affecting the brain, such as cerebral palsy, head injury or stroke, occurs with overactive bladder symptoms. 1.3.5 Consider them when urodynamic findings demonstrate impaired bladder storage. 1.3.6 After starting treatment, monitor residual urine in people not using intermittent or indwelling catheterisation. 1.3.7 Prescribing should account for possible central nervous system effects, including confusion, from antimuscarinics that cross the blood-brain barrier, such as oxybutynin; reduced bladder emptying and a potentially increased urinary tract infection risk; and new or worsened constipation.

document_sections.heading: Beta-3-adrenoceptor agonists
document_sections.content: 1.3.8 NICE technology appraisal guidance describes beta-3-adrenoceptor agonists as options for overactive bladder symptoms when antimuscarinics are unsuitable, insufficiently effective or cause unacceptable adverse effects. The cited guidance concerns vibegron (TA999, 2024) and mirabegron (TA290, 2013).

document_sections.heading: Botulinum toxin type A
document_sections.content: In August 2012, botulinum toxin type A lacked UK marketing authorisation for the indications in recommendations 1.3.9 to 1.3.12. 1.3.9 Offer bladder-wall injection to adults with spinal cord disease, such as spinal cord injury or multiple sclerosis, and overactive bladder symptoms when antimuscarinic drugs are ineffective or poorly tolerated. 1.3.10 Consider the same approach for children and young people with spinal cord disease and overactive bladder symptoms after ineffective or poorly tolerated antimuscarinics. 1.3.11 Offer injection to adults with spinal cord disease and urodynamically demonstrated impaired storage when antimuscarinics are ineffective or poorly tolerated. 1.3.12 Consider injection for children and young people meeting those latter conditions. 1.3.13 Before offering injection, explain to the person or their family and carers that most people with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction need a catheterisation regimen afterwards, and establish that they can and will manage one if retention occurs. 1.3.14 Monitor residual urine during treatment in people without a catheterisation regimen. 1.3.15 Monitor the upper urinary tract during treatment when renal complications are considered a risk, for example with high intravesical pressure on filling cystometry. 1.3.16 Ensure prompt repeat injections when symptoms recur for people offered ongoing treatment with repeated injections.

document_sections.heading: Augmentation cystoplasty
document_sections.content: 1.3.17 Consider augmentation cystoplasty with an intestinal segment for people with non-progressive neurological disorders and complications of impaired storage, such as hydronephrosis or incontinence, only following thorough clinical and urodynamic assessment and discussion of complications, risks and alternatives with the person or their family and carers. 1.3.18 Offer lifelong follow-up after the procedure because long-term complications can include metabolic effects, vitamin B12 deficiency and bladder cancer.

document_sections.heading: 1.4 Treatment for stress incontinence
document_sections.content: The treatment approaches discussed are pelvic floor muscle training, sling surgery and an artificial urinary sphincter.

document_sections.heading: Pelvic floor muscle training
document_sections.content: 1.4.1 Consider training when lower urinary tract dysfunction results from multiple sclerosis or stroke, or from another neurological condition with preserved voluntary pelvic floor contraction. Select patients after specialist pelvic floor assessment and consider adding biofeedback or pelvic floor electrical stimulation, or both.

document_sections.heading: Urethral tape and sling surgery
document_sections.content: 1.4.2 Consider autologous fascial sling surgery for neurogenic stress incontinence. 1.4.3 Do not routinely use synthetic tapes or slings for this condition because of urethral erosion risk.

document_sections.heading: Artificial urinary sphincter
document_sections.content: 1.4.4 Consider implantation for neurogenic stress incontinence only when an alternative, such as an autologous fascial sling, is less likely to provide control. 1.4.5 Discuss device risks, possible repeat operations and alternative procedures with the person or their family and carers, and confirm adequate low-pressure bladder storage capacity. 1.4.6 Monitor the upper urinary tract after implantation, for example by annual ultrasound, because storage function can worsen after treatment.

document_sections.heading: 1.5 Treatment to improve bladder emptying
document_sections.content: The recommendation in this section concerns alpha-blockers.

document_sections.heading: Alpha-blockers
document_sections.content: 1.5.1 Do not offer alpha-blockers to treat bladder-emptying problems caused by neurological disease.

document_sections.heading: 1.6 Management with catheter valves
document_sections.content: 1.6.1 A catheter valve may replace a drainage bag when appropriate; this recommendation comes from the NICE guideline on healthcare-associated infections in primary and community care. 1.6.2 When considering a valve instead of continuous bag drainage, assess the person's preferences, support from family and carers, manual dexterity, cognition and lower urinary tract function. 1.6.3 Consider continued upper urinary tract surveillance when storage is impaired, for example by reduced bladder compliance.

document_sections.heading: 1.7 Management with ileal conduit diversion
document_sections.content: 1.7.1 For neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction with major, intractable management difficulties, including incontinence or renal deterioration, consider ileal conduit diversion (urostomy) and discuss simultaneous cystectomy as prophylaxis against pyocystis.

document_sections.heading: 1.8 Treatment to prevent urinary tract infection
document_sections.content: 1.8.1 Do not routinely use antibiotic prophylaxis for urinary tract infections in neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction. 1.8.2 Consider prophylaxis after a recent history of frequent or severe infections. 1.8.3 Before prescribing it, investigate treatable urinary tract causes such as stones or incomplete emptying, discuss risks and benefits, and consult microbiologist-approved local protocols or a microbiologist about regimens. 1.8.4 Regularly reassess whether prophylaxis remains necessary. 1.8.5 At a change of a long-term indwelling urinary catheter, do not routinely offer antibiotic prophylaxis; consider it following previous symptomatic infection after a catheter change or when catheterisation causes trauma, defined as frank haematuria afterwards or 2 or more catheterisation attempts. In August 2012, no antibiotics had UK marketing authorisation for this catheter-change indication. The catheter-change recommendation comes from the NICE guideline on healthcare-associated infections in primary and community care.

document_sections.heading: 1.9 Monitoring and surveillance protocols
document_sections.content: 1.9.1 Do not use serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate alone to monitor renal function in neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction. 1.9.2 Consider isotopic glomerular filtration rate when precise measurement is required, for example if kidney imaging suggests compromised function. 1.9.3 Offer lifelong renal ultrasound surveillance for people judged at high risk of renal complications; annual or 2 yearly scans are examples. High-risk groups include spinal cord injury or spina bifida and adverse urodynamic findings such as impaired bladder compliance, detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia or vesico-ureteric reflux. 1.9.4 Do not use plain abdominal radiography for routine surveillance. 1.9.5 Consider urodynamic investigations within surveillance for people at high risk of urinary tract complications, including those with spina bifida, spinal cord injury or anorectal abnormalities. 1.9.6 Do not use cystoscopy routinely for surveillance. 1.9.7 Do not use renal scintigraphy routinely for surveillance.

document_sections.heading: 1.10 Potential complications: providing information and initial management
document_sections.content: This section addresses renal impairment, bladder stones and bladder cancer.

document_sections.heading: Renal impairment
document_sections.content: 1.10.1 Explain to the person and their family and carers the elevated risk of renal complications, including stones, hydronephrosis and scarring, with neurogenic urinary tract dysfunction, particularly with spina bifida or spinal cord injury. Describe warning symptoms such as loin pain, urinary tract infection and haematuria, and when to seek professional care. 1.10.2 During treatment discussions, explain that indwelling urethral catheters may carry a higher risk of renal complications, including stones and scarring, than methods such as intermittent self-catheterisation. 1.10.3 Investigate symptoms suggestive of upper urinary tract disease with renal imaging.

document_sections.heading: Bladder stones
document_sections.content: 1.10.4 Explain the increased bladder-stone risk in neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction and advise when symptoms such as recurrent infection, repeated catheter blockage or haematuria warrant professional assessment. 1.10.5 Explain that indwelling urethral and suprapubic catheters are associated with more bladder stones than other bladder-management methods, and describe the same warning symptoms. 1.10.6 Refer people with possible bladder stones, indicated for example by recurrent catheter blockages, repeated urinary tract infection or haematuria, for cystoscopy.

document_sections.heading: Bladder cancer
document_sections.content: 1.10.7 Explain that bladder cancer risk may be elevated with neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction, particularly after a long history of the condition with complicating factors such as recurrent urinary tract infections. Advise the person and their family and carers to seek professional care for warning symptoms, especially haematuria. 1.10.8 Use a suspected cancer pathway referral for urinary tract imaging and cystoscopy in people with visible haematuria, increased urinary tract infection frequency or other unexplained lower urinary tract symptoms.

document_sections.heading: 1.11 Access to and interaction with services
document_sections.content: The recommendations address communication with specialist services, written care information, continuity and transfer between paediatric and adult services.

document_sections.heading: Access to and interaction with services
document_sections.content: 1.11.1 Following specialised care for neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction, such as care in a spinal injury or paediatric urology unit, provide specialist-advice contact details to the person, family and carers, and involved non-specialist medical and nursing staff. 1.11.2 Give the person and their family and carers written details of key professionals, their responsibilities and contact information; copies of clinical correspondence; and lists of prescribed medicines and equipment. Send the same information to the person's GP. 1.11.3 Healthcare professionals should follow NICE patient-experience recommendations, particularly those concerning individually tailored services and continuity of care and relationships.

document_sections.heading: Transfer from child to adult services
document_sections.content: 1.11.4 For transition to adult care, establish a structured pathway early with the young person and parents or carers; involve parents and carers in transfer documentation with the young person's consent; give the person and receiving clinician a comprehensive account of history, investigations and treatments; incorporate multidisciplinary information; plan continuing urological services; and formally transfer responsibility to named individuals. 1.11.5 On receiving a person into adult care, review transfer records, coordinate with other involved adult services, provide service and key-staff contact details, and ensure continued urological provision. 1.11.6 Consider regular multidisciplinary meetings between paediatric and adult specialists to discuss care in the years before and after transition.

document_sections.heading: Alpha-blocking agents
document_sections.content: These medicines block alpha receptors and thereby inhibit responses to sympathetic impulses. Their inhibition of non-vascular smooth-muscle contraction at the bladder neck and prostate underlies their common use for male bladder outflow obstruction when urinary tract innervation is normal. Other names given are alpha adrenergic blocking agents and alpha adrenergic antagonists.

document_sections.heading: Antimuscarinic drugs
document_sections.content: These anticholinergic agents specifically block muscarinic cholinergic receptors. By reducing the response of bladder-wall muscle to stimulatory nerve signals, they are used to manage overactive bladder.

document_sections.heading: Augmentation cystoplasty
document_sections.content: This operation enlarges bladder capacity by reconstructing the bladder with an isolated segment of intestine.

document_sections.heading: Autologous fascial sling surgery
document_sections.content: For stress urinary incontinence, this operation supports the urethra with a harvested strip of rectus fascia.

document_sections.heading: Behavioural management programmes
document_sections.content: Behavioural therapies are generally used for urge or mixed urinary incontinence. Timed voiding uses scheduled toileting rather than waiting for perceived bladder filling. Bladder retraining progressively lengthens intervals between voids or asks the person to defer voiding for a specified time after urgency begins. Habit retraining identifies an individual's pattern and schedules toileting to precede expected leakage.

document_sections.heading: Biofeedback
document_sections.content: Instruments convey information about physiological activity so that a person can become aware of, and aim to control, those functions.

document_sections.heading: Bladder retraining
document_sections.content: This term refers to the approach defined under behavioural management programmes.

document_sections.heading: Bladder stone
document_sections.content: A bladder stone forms through crystallisation and accumulation of urinary salts and contains calcium or ammonium phosphate and oxalate salts. Formation typically accompanies urinary bacterial colonisation, such as with an indwelling catheter, or incomplete bladder emptying.

document_sections.heading: Cauda equina compression
document_sections.content: Compression of nerve roots in the lower spinal canal that supply the lower limbs, bladder and urethral sphincter is a serious condition.

document_sections.heading: Cystectomy
document_sections.content: Cystectomy removes some or all of the urinary bladder surgically.

document_sections.heading: Filling cystometry
document_sections.content: During this part of urodynamic testing, liquid is introduced slowly into the bladder while pressure and volume are measured to evaluate bladder function.

document_sections.heading: Habit retraining
document_sections.content: This term refers to the approach defined under behavioural management programmes.

document_sections.heading: Hydronephrosis
document_sections.content: The renal pelvis and calyces become distended and dilated, usually because urine cannot flow freely from the kidney. Without treatment, back pressure progressively causes renal atrophy.

document_sections.heading: Ileal conduit diversion
document_sections.content: After bladder removal, an isolated small-intestinal segment carries urine from the ureters to an abdominal-wall stoma.

document_sections.heading: Neurogenic
document_sections.content: The term describes something arising from nerves or nervous tissue.

document_sections.heading: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation
document_sections.content: Small electrical impulses delivered through the skin stimulate underlying nerves and muscles to cause involuntary contraction. The procedure can strengthen healthy muscle or preserve muscle mass during or after enforced inactivity, help maintain or improve range of motion, facilitate voluntary motor control and temporarily lessen spasticity when muscle innervation remains intact.

document_sections.heading: Overactive bladder
document_sections.content: This condition produces urinary urgency, whether or not accompanied by urge incontinence, usually with more frequent urination. Involuntary bladder contractions or bladder spasms usually cause the sudden, strong need to void.

document_sections.heading: Pelvic floor muscle training
document_sections.content: Daily exercises strengthen muscles supporting the uterus, bladder and other pelvic organs and help prevent unintended urinary leakage. The document also calls them Kegel exercises or pelvic muscle rehabilitation.

document_sections.heading: Pelvic floor prolapse
document_sections.content: Reduced muscle tone or ligament elasticity, or both, permits the uterus or other pelvic organs to descend into the vagina; severe prolapse may extend beyond the vaginal opening.

document_sections.heading: Pressure-flow studies
document_sections.content: Bladder pressure and urine flow are measured simultaneously during voiding to assess emptying. Low flow alongside raised voiding pressure can, for example, identify bladder outflow obstruction.

document_sections.heading: Prompted voiding
document_sections.content: This behavioural programme encourages a person to initiate toileting, usually through positive reinforcement and education of the person and their carers.

document_sections.heading: Renal scintigraphy
document_sections.content: A gamma camera records the distribution of an injected radioisotope that accumulates in the kidneys, producing images of renal structure and function.

document_sections.heading: Sacral agenesis
document_sections.content: Failure of normal sacral-spine development leaves part or all of the sacrum absent. In many cases, some or all nerves supplying pelvic organs also develop abnormally.

document_sections.heading: Spina bifida
document_sections.content: The spinal bones fail to close during fetal development. With myelomeningocele, abnormal development also affects the spinal cord or nerves and their covering membranes, disrupting innervation of the lower limbs and pelvic organs.

document_sections.heading: Spinal dysraphism
document_sections.content: This collective term covers developmental abnormalities of the spine and spinal cord, including spina bifida.

document_sections.heading: Stress incontinence
document_sections.content: Stress urinary incontinence can refer to a symptom, sign or diagnosis, but urodynamic stress incontinence can be diagnosed only after urodynamic investigation. It involves involuntary urine leakage when abdominal pressure increases without a detrusor contraction.

document_sections.heading: Suspected cancer pathway referral
document_sections.content: Following an urgent GP referral for suspected cancer, the person receives either a cancer diagnosis or its exclusion within 28 days.

document_sections.heading: Timed voiding
document_sections.content: This term refers to the approach defined under behavioural management programmes.

document_sections.heading: Urethral tape and sling surgery
document_sections.content: These operations aim to restore control when coughing or exercise causes leakage. Tape surgery positions a thin artificial mesh ribbon beneath the urethra to support it and maintain continence. Sling surgery places a sling around the urethra, lifts it towards its usual position and applies pressure to aid urine retention; the sling attaches to the abdominal wall.

document_sections.heading: Urodynamic investigations
document_sections.content: These investigations combine clinical assessment with physical measures, including urinary pressure and flow, to evaluate bladder and urethral function. Video-urodynamic assessment fills the bladder with dye so X-rays can be taken during filling and emptying.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations for research
document_sections.content: The guideline development group identifies research questions on antimuscarinics, botulinum toxin, prevention of symptomatic urinary tract infections and long-term bladder-management strategies.

document_sections.heading: 1 Safety and efficacy of antimuscarinics
document_sections.content: The proposed research would compare the safety and efficacy of newer antimuscarinics for neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction against (a) placebo/usual care and (b) other antimuscarinics.

document_sections.heading: Why this is important
document_sections.content: High-quality clinical trials of newer antimuscarinics in neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction have not been conducted; placebo-controlled and head-to-head evidence is lacking. Their efficacy in this population is unknown, they cost more, and claims of fewer adverse effects relate to the non-neurogenic population. Adverse effects largely arise outside the bladder, including dry mouth. Concern is growing that central nervous system effects could impair cognition in children with brain damage due to cerebral palsy or hydrocephalus and in adults with cognitive impairment due to cerebral involvement in multiple sclerosis or neurodegenerative disease.

document_sections.heading: 2 Safety and efficacy of botulinum toxin
document_sections.content: The research question compares botulinum toxin with (a) usual care, (b) antimuscarinics and (c) augmentation cystoplasty in neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction.

document_sections.heading: Why this is important
document_sections.content: Research is needed on sustained efficacy after repeated intradetrusor botulinum toxin type A injections, including continence and upper urinary tract preservation. Detrusor injection effectively manages incontinence and improves urodynamic storage measures, with potential renal protection against high intravesical pressure; it is well tolerated across conditions and ages. Efficacy over many injections remains unestablished. A trial should assess continence, renal preservation and quality of life over repeated cycles in children and adults whose kidneys are anatomically normal on imaging and whose renal function is normal. The effects should also be studied in cerebral conditions associated with urinary dysfunction as well as spinal cord injury, spina bifida and multiple sclerosis; evidence in other conditions is limited to small patient numbers in heterogeneous case series. Successful treatment of cerebral disease might avoid antimuscarinic-associated cognitive impairment. A trial in primary cerebral conditions should include, but not be limited to, stroke, head injury and cerebral palsy, exclude multiple sclerosis, and enrol both children and adults. Alongside the primary outcomes of continence, upper urinary tract preservation and quality of life, it should measure tolerability, acceptability, carer burden and carer quality of life.

document_sections.heading: 3 Management strategies to reduce the risk of symptomatic urinary tract infections
document_sections.content: The research question asks which strategies, including prophylactic antibiotics and invasive or non-invasive aids to bladder drainage, reduce symptomatic urinary tract infections in neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction.

document_sections.heading: Why this is important
document_sections.content: Recurrent infections cause substantial morbidity: they may worsen incontinence, cause malaise or involve the upper urinary tract with possible renal-function loss. In multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease and dementia, infection-related temperature rises can worsen neurological function and can even trigger a multiple sclerosis relapse. Contributing factors include loss of normal bladder function, high intravesical pressures and incomplete emptying; intermittent or permanent catheterisation inevitably worsens the problem. Research has difficulty separating asymptomatic bacterial colonisation from infection. Because infections impose a major clinical burden and antibiotic resistance is a global concern, it is important to determine whether preventive strategies, including patient training or information about prophylactic antibiotics, reduce symptomatic infection.

document_sections.heading: 4 Bladder management strategies
document_sections.content: The research question concerns long-term risks and quality-of-life effects of different bladder-management strategies in neurological disease.

document_sections.heading: Why this is important
document_sections.content: Available strategies include permanent urethral or suprapubic catheterisation, intermittent self-catheterisation, penile sheath collection systems and pads. Evidence on acceptability to patients, families and carers is very sparse; existing research mainly concerns spinal injury and may apply to other neurological diseases. These long-term methods affect health and quality of life, so informed choice requires evidence about benefits and risks. Little evidence establishes which methods are most likely to cause renal impairment, urinary stones, infections, hydronephrosis or bladder malignancy, and comparative quality-of-life effects for patients, families and carers are unknown. Research is complicated by heterogeneous neurological conditions, long treatment courses and cognitive impairment in some groups. Proposed prospective disease-specific cohorts could compare methods using generic and disease-specific quality-of-life measures and prospective screening for renal impairment, stones and infection. Family and carer quality of life deserves particular attention, especially when they care for someone with cognitive impairment.

document_sections.heading: Context
document_sections.content: The lower urinary tract comprises bladder and urethra and coordinates urine storage and expulsion under central and peripheral nervous-system control. Neurological disease affecting the brain, suprasacral or sacral spinal cord, or peripheral nerves can produce characteristic patterns of bladder and sphincter dysfunction; the nature of the injury also matters. Childhood neurological damage often stems from congenital conditions such as spina bifida or sacral agenesis. Stroke, spinal cord injury and cauda equina compression can cause relatively stable injury, whereas dementia, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis and peripheral neuropathy can cause progressive damage. Table 1 groups example neurological conditions by lesion site and likelihood of progression. Because the neural centres governing urinary, bowel and sexual function are close, dysfunctions often coexist and warrant a holistic rather than isolated urinary approach. Neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction can impair storage, emptying or both; storage symptoms include increased frequency and incontinence. Urinary symptoms can cause embarrassment, social isolation and difficulty with daily activities. Incontinence can result from overactive bladder, urethral sphincter dysfunction or both. Risks include markedly more urinary tract infections and loss of renal function from elevated bladder pressures, infection or kidney stones. Medical treatment often does not restore normal urinary function, and medicines, intermittent self-catheterisation, indwelling catheters, pads and appliances can affect quality of life. Families and carers may face physical, psychological, relationship and social pressures. Costs arise from supplies, medicines, operations, care and professional support, as well as effects on employment, follow-up and long-term surveillance. The full guideline contains 3 algorithms outlining the clinical approach. For recommended uses outside UK marketing authorisation at publication, prescribers should follow relevant professional guidance, take responsibility for the decision, and obtain and document informed consent.
